> Text-to-image by citation of real COCO instances, self-verified; GenEval-style 50.9% held-out, no generative model.

# Oracle7-Artist 2.0 (internal)

**Status:** public release. Prometheus7 Research Institute, 2026-09-25. **Held-out complete: GenEval-style 50.9% (2,212 images, run once).**
**Frozen 2026-09-25 13:35 UTC** (box four `/opt/oracle7-artist/results/HELDOUT_FREEZE.txt`):
- code SHA-256 `000154e2ebf0403c300c98c12da0aa94a7e553e12e07acab12b74086f8acd6c7` (C-locale sorted `artist/*.py` +
  `eval/*.py`, v0 copies excluded);
- library index SHA-256 `4b1d83af4ab12424822ce58129fd044283fa77d216bac789784c80f062187f4d` (2,673 sprites, 80
  classes).

## What it is

Text-to-image by citation, with no generative model and no learned weights.
1. **Parse.** A prompt is parsed into objects, counts, colours and spatial relations.
2. **Cite.** Every object is a real instance cut from COCO val2017, cited by image id and annotation id.
3. **Lay out.** The layout satisfies counts and relations by construction.
4. **Colour.** It cites a real instance already of the named colour when the library holds one. Otherwise it
   recolours an instance, keeping its light and saturation structure.
5. **Verify.** Artist re-measures every clause from its own pixels.

**The judge is independent of Artist** and shares no code with it. It is OWLv2 (base) queried with all 80 COCO class
names plus CLIP ViT-B/32 for colour, applying GenEval's task rules. It is an **approximation** of the official GenEval
scorer (Mask2Former + CLIP); numbers are "GenEval-style", not official GenEval. Its detection threshold (0.25) was set
by presence F1 on 250 real COCO photographs before library v1 existed. It was then fixed.

## Protocol

- **Development:** 120 templated prompts (seed 4242) covering the GenEval task families, excluding every official
  prompt. Every library and renderer change was made here.
- **Held-out:** the 553 official GenEval prompts × seeds 0–3, rendered and judged **once**, seed-major.
  `results/geneval_heldout.json` is rewritten after each seed and marked `final: true` at the end.

## Development results (120 prompts, seed 0)

| Version | Overall | Counting | Two objects | Position | Colours | Colour attribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v0 (first 40 prompts, thr 0.30) | 39.2% | 75% | 37.5% | 33.3% | 50% | 0% |
| v1 (library filters, own-colour citation) | 45.5% | 68.0% | 58.3% | 52.6% | 48.4% | 0% |
| **v1b, frozen** (texture-keeping recolour, fragmented masks rejected) | **47.7%** | 68.0% | 58.3% | 52.6% | 45.2% | 14.3% |

Artist's self-verification passes 95–100% of its own images in every task. **The gap between self-verification and the
judge is the finding:** the layout is right by construction, but many composited instances are not recognised as that
object by a detector trained on photographs.

What changed from v0 to v1b, each change found by looking at dev renders:
- **Occlusion:** occluded instances are dropped (other boxes may cover at most 35% of the instance's box).
- **Legibility:** dark or flat cut-outs are dropped (median value < 0.18, or std < 0.04).
- **Fragmentation:** masks whose largest piece is under 80% of the mask are dropped.
- **Own colour:** a sprite's own colour is recorded only when unambiguous (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, white,
  black; saturation ≥ 0.35).
- **Recolour:** it now keeps the object's own light and saturation ratios. The old recolour flattened objects into
  blobs.

## Held-out (official GenEval prompts): complete

Run once on box four, 2026-09-25 13:35 to 22:33 UTC (32,275 s on 2 CPU cores, no GPU): the 553 official prompts × seeds
0–3 = 2,212 images, judged once. `results/geneval_heldout.json` (`final: true`, SHA-256
`b792e7906e54171d31ca3e3e5134c6250d481c5e9e44af288dc98f0f4c0cda9e`). The code and library hashes are the frozen ones above.

| Task | Images | Independent judge | Artist's own self-check |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Overall (GenEval-style)** | **2,212** | **50.9%** | |
| Single object | 320 | 80.6% | 100% |
| Two objects | 396 | 49.2% | 100% |
| Counting | 320 | 55.0% | 91.3% |
| Colours | 376 | 45.7% | 97.1% |
| Position | 400 | 56.0% | 100% |
| Colour attribution | 400 | 19.0% | 92.0% |

584 of the 2,212 images needed a recoloured instance. Held-out (50.9%) is above the frozen dev figure (47.7%), so the dev
prompts did not overstate it.

Published GenEval overall scores for generative models (official scorer): SD 1.5 ≈ 43%, SDXL ≈ 55%, SD3 ≈ 68–74%. Artist
uses no generative model and no learned weights, and every object in every image is a cited COCO instance. The judge is
an approximation of the official scorer, so this comparison is indicative only.

## Failures, stated plainly

- **Most dev failures are "missing":** the judge does not detect the composited object. Colour attribution is weakest
  (14.3%). Two recoloured objects in one image compound the detector's difficulty.
- **Counting fails when an instance overlaps or is cropped** below the detector's confidence (8/25 dev).
- **Thin library classes:** hair drier 1, toaster 2, skis 3, frisbee 5, remote 5, knife 6.
- **Brown, purple and pink objects are always recoloured,** because photographed objects in these hues are read
  unreliably (red apples read as pink or purple).
- **Judge calibration overlap:** 67 of the 250 calibration photographs are also cited by the frozen library. The
  threshold was chosen on whole-photo detection before that library existed, so this does not favour Artist. It is
  disclosed.
- **The judge is not the official GenEval scorer.** Treat comparisons with published GenEval numbers (SD 1.5 ≈ 43%,
  SDXL ≈ 55%, SD3 ≈ 68–74%) as indicative only.

## Reproduce (box four)

```
cd /opt/oracle7-artist
judge-venv/bin/python artist/build_library.py coco library
judge-venv/bin/python eval/calibrate_judge.py 250
judge-venv/bin/python eval/eval_geneval.py dev 120
judge-venv/bin/python eval/eval_geneval.py heldout
```

# Oracle7-infrastructure

An AI that adapts to whatever it is pointed at. Installed on a system, Oracle7 finds out what is there, decides what to
read, builds the same set of readers for everything it finds, and learns from that system's own future which forecasts it
can trust. Every value it holds keeps the place it was read from. It proposes actions with a predicted effect and a dry run,
runs nothing until a person approves it, and then checks whether the effect happened.

It contains no neural network. It is one Python file that uses only the standard library.

## How it adapts

- **To what is there.** On each system it discovers the services, scheduled jobs, websites, certificates and ports by itself.
  The four servers it was first installed on held between 36 and 106 services each; it needed no configuration for any of them.
- **To what it reads.** Readers are generated for every signal it finds, so a new service or website is covered from its
  first reading.
- **To how each system behaves.** Forecasting methods are admitted per signal and per system, only after they have beaten
  "nothing changes" on that system's own future. On the first day it admitted a trend method for certificate expiry on one
  server, where the value falls steadily, and kept the simpler assumption everywhere the trend had not earned it.
- **To other kinds of system.** Anything that publishes numbers can be added as a source: JSON over HTTP, Prometheus metrics,
  or the output of a command. Those values get the same readers, forecasts and gate.

## Install

```
sudo sh install.sh
python3 /opt/o7infra/o7infra_agent.py brief
python3 /opt/o7infra/desk.py "what is failing"
```

Requirements: Linux with systemd, Python 3.10 or later, root (to read the journal and service state). Optional: nginx (its
sites and certificates are found automatically), openssl (certificate expiry).

## What it does

**Finds what to watch.** With no configuration it lists the system's long-running services, its scheduled jobs, the websites
nginx serves with their TLS certificates, and its listening ports.

**Reads it.** Host load, CPU, memory and swap; space and inodes on every disk; network traffic; for every service its state,
memory, CPU and restart rate; whether every scheduled job's last run succeeded; journal errors per service; days left on every
certificate; whether every website answers and how fast. Every value is stored as time, entity, signal, value and source.

**Stays small.** Raw values are kept 24 hours and ten-minute means 30 days, under a hard size cap (60 MB by default). The
service unit limits it to 10% of one CPU and 150 MB of memory at the lowest CPU and I/O priority.

**Reads every signal the same way.** For whatever it finds it generates the same readers: current value, trend, time to
threshold, anomaly against the signal's own history, and which signals shifted just before an event.

**Tests its forecasts on the future.** Every forecast is recorded when it is made and scored when its time arrives. A
forecasting method is admitted for a kind of signal only after at least 30 scored forecasts beat the assumption that nothing
changes by at least 10%. Until then its forecasts are labelled unproven. `o7infra_agent.py gate` shows the current record.

**Proposes actions with their evidence.** Each proposal carries the reading that prompted it, the expected effect and the
output of a dry run. `approve <id>` then `execute <id>` runs one. After it runs, the agent checks the expected effect against
the next readings. An action type may run without approval only after five executions whose effect matched, and only when the
operator sets `O7INFRA_AUTONOMOUS=1`. By default it is off.

## First deployment

Installed on four of our own servers on 12 October 2026. Within the first hour:

- It found 278 services, 165 scheduled jobs, 102 websites, 56 TLS certificates and 182 listening ports, with no configuration.
- It held 2,551 current readings, of which 39 were critical and 2 warnings.
- Six services were in crash loops, restarting between 63 and 695 times an hour; one had restarted 144,690 times in total.
- Two websites were down: one returning 502, one not answering.
- One server was at 97.3% disk and 100% swap.
- Certificate renewal was failing on two servers. Reading the certificates showed the soonest expiry was 51.5 days away.
- One website looked down because it does not answer HEAD requests. The agent now retries with GET; it answered 200.

Each finding is shown with its source, for example `systemctl show NRestarts=144690`, `HTTPS HEAD status 502` or
`openssl x509 /etc/letsencrypt/live/<site>/fullchain.pem`.

The same day:

- Two proposed actions were approved and run (clearing old system logs on two servers). The agent then measured their effect
  from its own readings: free disk went from 4.616 to 5.507 GB on one server and from 1.062 to 1.341 GB on the other. On the
  second server the log tool's own summary reported that it had freed nothing; the agent records what it measured. Both
  effects matched the prediction.
- 1,242 forecasts had been scored against what then happened. The gate admitted one method for one signal (certificate
  expiry, on one server) and refused the trend method wherever it had done worse than assuming no change.

## Talking to it

```
python3 /opt/o7infra/desk.py "when will the disk fill"
python3 /opt/o7infra/desk.py "when do certificates expire"
python3 /opt/o7infra/desk.py "what should I do"
python3 /opt/o7infra/desk.py --repl
```

Questions outside the system can go to the Oracle7 core if you have it:
`desk.py --oracle7 /path/to/oracle7-slim "<question>"`. See [oracle7-slim](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-slim) and [oracle7](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7).

## Other systems

Anything that publishes numbers can be read by adding it to `/etc/o7infra/sources.json`: JSON over HTTP (a value by its
path), Prometheus metrics (by name pattern), or the output of a command (by pattern). See `sources.example.json`. Those
values get the same readers, forecasts and gate.

Several servers: `fleet.py host1 host2 ...` asks each host's agent over SSH and prints one view.

## The Oracle7 family

Oracle7-infrastructure is one of several systems built the same way: read what is there, keep a receipt for every reading,
admit a method only after it is measured, and decline what cannot be checked. Each was frozen and then measured once on
data it had not seen.

| Pointed at | Repository | Held-out result, measured once |
|---|---|---|
| Servers and services | oracle7-infrastructure (this) | first deployment above |
| Questions, with 267 domain specialists | [oracle7](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7), [oracle7-slim](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-slim) | sealed release test 17: 111 right, 5 wrong, 1 false yes of 150 (slim: 108 / 3 / 1); precision 95.3% / 97.5% |
| Simulated spacecraft faults | [oracle7-deepspace](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-deepspace) | right action in 98.9% of 1,700 fresh scenarios, none harmful; a simplified limit-to-safe-mode baseline 29.4% |
| Routing decisions | [oracle7-trafficcop](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-trafficcop) | 30 of 32 held-out cases; both misses were abstentions |
| Website and repository reconstruction | [oracle7-chameleon](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-chameleon) | 1 of 4 held-out repositories complete on first pass; 0 false completions |
| Images | [oracle7-vision](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-vision) | MNIST 98.6%, Fashion-MNIST 90.5%, CIFAR-10 63.0%; ScreenSpot clicks 21.3% |
| Text to image | [oracle7-artist](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7-artist) | GenEval-style 50.9% on 2,212 images, every object a cited COCO instance |

None of them uses a neural network at inference. Each repository states its failures alongside its results.

## Limits

- Forecasts are unproven until the gate has scored enough of them on each system; on the first day most were still unproven.
- Actions are recommendations unless a person approves them. Two actions have been run and verified so far.
- Tested on four Linux servers running systemd. The sources file has not yet been used on outside systems.
- Each host runs its own agent; `fleet.py` joins them by SSH.
- Website checks request the site's home page only.

## Licence

Apache-2.0. Oracle7's core and its knowledge stores are released separately under their own terms.

> Image recognition, text reading and GUI grounding by cited exemplars over fixed descriptors; no learned weights.

# Oracle7-Vision 2.0 (internal)

**Status:** public release. Prometheus7 Research Institute, 2026-09-25.
**Source SHA-256** (sorted `vision/*.py` + `eval/*.py` on box four, `/opt/oracle7-vision`):
`b796b4eeff80115425d97fa0157e0dcc09187c698ca87e950d10a19891199a02` (the final code, including `vision/screen.py`;
the C-locale sorted concatenation of `vision/*.py` and `eval/*.py`). Each result file also carries the SHA of the code
that produced it. The exemplar results were produced by `9f571b4b…` (before the glyph and chart modules were
added; the exemplar path itself is unchanged).

## What it is

Vision has no trained weights. An image is described by fixed descriptors:
- HOG at two cell sizes,
- LBP texture histograms,
- an HSV colour histogram,
- a small thumbnail.

Each descriptor group goes through a seeded random projection and is bound to a role vector by circular convolution
(HRR, D = 2048). The groups are then bundled into one vector. Recognition is a k-nearest-neighbour vote over a store of
labelled exemplars.

Each answer cites the store indices that voted for it. When the vote margin falls below a threshold chosen on the dev
split, Vision abstains.

Text is read by synthesis:
- Glyphs are rendered in many open-licence fonts.
- Their geometry is measured against the baseline and cap height.
- A line is segmented by recognition (dynamic programming over merge/split atoms).
- Tokens are repaired with digit/letter maps.

Chart questions are answered by fixed rules over the words Vision has read and positioned: axis ticks, legend,
bar/label alignment.

## Protocol (fixed before any held-out data was read)

| Task | Development | Held-out, scored once |
|---|---|---|
| Classification (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100; Hugging Face parquet, official splits) | last 10% of official train; store = first 90% | official test; store = full train |
| Text reading (rendered lines) | store font families, seeds 0–199 | font families the store has never seen (fixed hash split), fresh seeds 20000–20399 |
| ChartQA (HuggingFaceM4/ChartQA) | val split | official test split (2,500: 1,250 human + 1,250 augmented) |

Every accuracy is reported with a Wilson 95% CI.

Classification is checked by an instrument mutant: the store labels are shuffled, and accuracy must fall to chance.

## Results (held-out)

### Classification: full coverage, accuracy [95% CI]

| Dataset | Vision | Raw-pixel kNN | Nearest class mean | Mutant (chance) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MNIST | **98.58%** [98.33, 98.79] | 97.56% | 91.12% | 10.18% (10%) |
| Fashion-MNIST | **90.46%** [89.87, 91.02] | 87.00% | 74.76% | 9.84% (10%) |
| CIFAR-10 | **62.99%** [62.04, 63.93] | 46.22% | 43.85% | 10.26% (10%) |
| CIFAR-100 | **35.38%** [34.45, 36.32] | 22.37% | 23.44% | 0.99% (1%) |

Selective accuracy uses the thresholds that gave 70% coverage on dev:

| Dataset | Held-out coverage | Accuracy on answered |
|---|---|---|
| Fashion-MNIST | 69.3% | 98.77% |
| CIFAR-10 | 68.1% | 76.39% |
| CIFAR-100 | 70.6% | 45.58% |

MNIST's vote margin saturates: at both dev thresholds, 90.7% of test images are answered at 99.85% accuracy.

Queries take about 2–2.6 ms on one CPU. The store is 410–490 MB.

### Text reading in unseen fonts: character error rate (lower is better)

| Reader | CER | Exact line |
|---|---|---|
| v0, first held-out run (seeds 10000–10399, since retired) | 0.3025 | 4.3% |
| Shape only (geometry weight 0) | 0.2615 | 6.25% |
| **v1** | **0.1955** | **20.0%** |
| v1 on development fonts | 0.1237 | 34.5% |

The held-out fonts are Caladea, Carlito, Latin Modern Roman Demi, Mulish, Oswald, Raleway and Roboto.

### ChartQA test (relaxed accuracy, the standard metric)

| Split | Accuracy | Coverage | Accuracy on answered |
|---|---|---|---|
| All 2,500 | **3.64%** | 33.8% | 10.8% |
| Human questions | 1.68% | | |
| Augmented questions | 5.60% | | |

By rule (n answered): lookup 27.0% (226), argmax label 13.5% (52), min 7.6% (53), max 5.6% (215), max−min 5.3% (38),
average 3.1% (131), count 1.0% (101). There were 1,652 abstentions.

### ScreenSpot: GUI grounding (instruction + screenshot → click; correct = inside the target box)

- **Data:** `bevaya/ScreenSpot`, the renamed `rootsautomation/ScreenSpot`, 1,272 items.
- **Split, fixed before any scoring:** dev = index % 5 == 0 (255 items); held-out = the other 1,017, scored once.
- **Threshold:** the dev sweep chose 0.0. Abstaining counts as wrong, and answering beat abstaining at every
  threshold.
- **Code SHA:** `b796b4eeff80115425d97fa0157e0dcc09187c698ca87e950d10a19891199a02`.

| | Held-out click accuracy | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| **Vision, all 1,017** | **21.34%** [18.93, 23.96] | 53.4% (39.96% right on answered) |
| Text targets (569) | 36.0% | 64.9% |
| Icon targets (448) | 2.7% | 38.8% |
| Mobile / desktop / web | 29.9% / 18.4% / 13.8% | |
| Baseline: click the screen centre | 2.46% | |
| Baseline: click a random read token | 2.95% | |
| Dev (255) | 21.2% | 48.6% |

Published click accuracy on the same benchmark: GPT-4V 16.2%, CogAgent 47.4%, SeeClick 53.4%.

Method (`vision/screen.py`):
1. Each pixel is compared with its local background, so text of either polarity becomes dark on white.
2. Components that cannot be glyphs (taller than 48 px or wider than 120 px) are erased.
3. The glyph reader reads the tokens.
4. The instruction's content words are matched to token spans by edit similarity, and the click is the centre of the
   best span.

The first dev run was killed for memory at 100 items. The fixes changed only resource use:
- a pixel bound on reader upscaling (off by default, so the OCR and ChartQA paths are unchanged),
- streaming parquet batches,
- a chunked glyph classifier that computes each row identically.

## Failures, stated plainly

- **ChartQA is weak.** Published multimodal LLMs score 60–90% on ChartQA; Vision scores 3.6%. The rule set covers only a
  third of the questions. On the questions it does answer it is right about one time in ten, because reading real chart
  images is far below the rendered-line OCR number. Human-written questions need reasoning the rule set does not have.
  This result is the honest floor of the method, not a competitive score.
- **CIFAR is far from learned models.** Fixed descriptors plus kNN reach 63% on CIFAR-10 and 35% on CIFAR-100. Trained
  CNNs exceed 95%. The gains over raw pixels (+16.8 and +13.0 points) are real; the absolute level is not competitive.
- **Text reading is on rendered lines, not photographs or scans.** A CER of 0.20 in unseen fonts is a measurement on
  clean synthetic text at 11–26 px. Typical errors are merged words ("JulyConodo"), extra spaces inside numbers
  ("1 1 1.49") and o/a confusions.
- **ScreenSpot icons: 2.7%.** An icon target has no text to read, and the method has no icon vocabulary. Among text
  targets, wrong clicks are mostly a second occurrence of the same word (a heading instead of a menu item), or a
  partial match ("To help" for "need some help").
- **Not evaluated:** DocVQA, VQAv2, TextVQA. The method has no component for open-ended visual questions. These are the
  next scope, and they are not claimed.

## What the evidence supports

On standard benchmarks, a deterministic descriptor + HRR + exemplar-kNN recogniser with no learned weights:
- beats raw-pixel and class-mean baselines on all four classification sets;
- abstains usefully (accuracy rises sharply as coverage falls);
- cites the training exemplars behind each answer;
- is verified by a shuffled-label mutant that falls to chance.

Its text reader transfers to font families it has never seen, with an error rate that fell from 0.30 to 0.20 between
v0 and v1, measured on fresh seeds.

The same reader grounds GUI instructions on real screenshots at 21.3%: more than seven times the centre and
random-token baselines and above published GPT-4V, with the gap to trained grounding models (SeeClick 53.4%) almost entirely on
icons.

venv/bin/python eval/eval_exemplar.py <mnist|fashion|cifar10|cifar100>
venv/bin/python eval/eval_glyph_ocr.py

# oracle7-slim

**Oracle7 is an AI built to say "I can't verify that" rather than guess.** It is not a neural language model. It answers
from stored, sourced records and from 267 specialists, each of which passed its own held-out test before it was allowed to
answer. Every reply carries its **path**: the route, specialists and records that produced it. When nothing in it can
verify an answer, it declines and tells you why. It does not always manage that: the measured section below says exactly
how often it is still wrong, and on what.

This is the **slim** release: the same core, routes and 267 specialists, with the smaller stores (Simple English Wikipedia, Wiktionary, WordNet, ConceptNet, Wikidata relations) and **no non-commercial material**, so it can be used commercially under the licences in DATA_LICENSES.md. The full release adds the deep Wikipedia/DBpedia/OpenStax stores; slim declines more often on open trivia.

- Download: **2.7 GB** (unpacks to 7.3 GB, every store checked against its published hash)
- Runs on: CPU only, Python 3.12, about 2 GB RAM; no GPU, no network access at run time
- Head: `oracle_release_runtime_w540` (the core the gate admitted when this was built; the site adds an input typo-repair layer that is not included)

## Quickstart

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python oracle7.py "A van gets 25 mpg. How many kg of CO2 does a 200-mile trip produce?"
python oracle7.py --repl          # a conversation (follow-ups work)
python oracle7.py --serve 8077    # local HTTP: POST /chat {"text": "..."}
python oracle7.py --workbench       # the Workbench: a local page (below)
python oracle7.py help              # every terminal command: ask, chat, specialists, verify, exam, scan, sensors...
```

The first run unpacks the stores (`--setup` does only that). Example reply:

```
The answer is 71.096 kg. (path: core_math → carboncapture → core_math)
  [answered] path: network>core_math carboncapture core_math
```

A `withheld` status is a deliberate decline, and its reply says why (for example: no admitted record answers it, a given is
not a physical amount, or a step of the path could not be checked).


## The Workbench

```bash
python oracle7.py --workbench     # opens http://127.0.0.1:8177/
```

A local page for your copy of Oracle7, laid out as a studio:
- the conversation on the left, under a diagram of the whole model that lights the path each answer takes;
- a workspace on the right;
- a live log of every turn, route and exam.

Ask it "what can you do?", or type `/help`, for every feature and command.

- **Start:** scan this computer, connect a server over SSH with your own key, add your tables and notes, or connect an MCP
  server. Each becomes a reader that names where every value came from (the call, the command, the file row or line, the
  tool and its arguments).
- **Sensors:** connect an HTTP device or hub (JSON or Prometheus metrics), an MQTT topic, a USB/serial device or a log
  file, or try a simulated node. Readings are kept 24 hours on your machine; answers give the value, its age, its source
  and whether it was measured, and a physically impossible reading is rejected and named.
- **Conversations:** kept on your machine in a side panel; reopen one and the core picks up its context. Any
  conversation can become a temporary specialist that recalls it.

from stored, sourced records and from 267 specialists, each of which passed its own held-out test before it was allowed to

## What it is

A decision service: given a state and a set of options, it returns one choice with a receipt. It contains no neural
network. It works in this order:
1. Admissibility preconditions strike options that cannot apply.
2. Obligations bind what must be done.
3. An evidence table of attested outcomes ranks what remains.
4. A short microfold lookahead breaks ties.
5. When nothing is warranted, it abstains to `collect_evidence`.

It replaces Laya, an LLM decision service, behind the same DecisionRequest contract. Standard library only; about
0.1 ms per decision.

# Oracle7 specialists

Community specialists for [Oracle7](https://huggingface.co/psiloceyeben/oracle7). Each file in `specialists/` is one
specialist, packaged by the Workbench's Share button as `<id>-<hash>.zip`. Inside the zip is a single folder: the
specialist's files and a `SHARE_MANIFEST.json` listing the SHA-256 of every file.

The 307 specialists that ship with the release are in the model repository, not here.

## Add yours

Only an admitted specialist can be packaged, meaning it passed its held-out exam on your computer. In the Workbench,
open Share and package it; the Workbench prints the zip's path. Then open a pull request to this dataset:

```bash
hf upload psiloceyeben/oracle7-specialists <path-to-zip> specialists/<zip-name> --repo-type dataset --create-pr
```

`hf` comes with `pip install huggingface_hub` (version 0.34 or later). The command the Workbench prints in this release uses the older `huggingface-cli` name and `Prometheus7/oracle7-specialists`; use the line above instead.

A pull request is merged when the zip opens, its files match its manifest, and the specialist passes its exam again here.

## Use one

Download a zip and import it in the Workbench (Specialists, then Import). The Workbench checks every file against the
manifest and refuses the package if one differs. The specialist's own verdict is kept as `shared_verdict_*.json`; it
takes the exam again on your computer before it answers anything.

## On-chain registration

A specialist can also be registered on Solana from the Workbench's Share tab: one transaction, signed in your own wallet,
burns 1 $ORACLE7 and writes a memo with the specialist's file hash, exam verdict and held-out score. Anyone can check a
specialist against its registration with the Check button or `python oracle7.py registry <id>`. Registration is optional
for a pull request here.
